source_text: Ἐκεῖνό γε μὴν κἂν ἐπαινέσειέ τις τοῦ κακοῦ, ὅτι ὅσῳπερ ἂν σφοδρότερος κινηθῇ, τοσούτῳ χαλεπώτερός ἐστι τῷ κεκτημένῳ. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τῶν βελῶν τὰ βιαίως φερό μενα, ἐπειδὰν καρτερῷ τινι καὶ ἀντιτύπῳ προσπέσῃ, ἐπὶ τὸν προέμενον ἐπανέρχεται· οὕτω καὶ τὰ τοῦ φθόνου κινήματα, οὐδὲν λυποῦντα τὸν βασκαινόμενον, αὐτοῦ πληγαὶ γίνονται τοῦ βασκάνου. Τίς γὰρ λυπούμενος ἠλάττωσέ ποτε τὰ τοῦ πλησίον καλά; Ἑαυτὸν μέντοι προσανάλωσε ταῖς λύπαις κατατηκόμενος. Ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῶν ἰοβόλων αὐτῶν ὀλεθριώτεροι εἶναι οἱ νοσοῦντες τὴν βασκανίαν ὑπονε νόηνται· εἴπερ τὰ μὲν διὰ πληγῆς ἐνίησι τὸν ἰὸν, καὶ κατὰ μικρὸν σηπεδόσι τὸ δηχθὲν ἐπινέμεται· τοὺς δὲ φθονερούς τινες οἴονται καὶ δι' ὀφθαλμῶν μόνων τὴν βλάβην ἐπιβάλλειν· ὥστε τὰ εὐεκτικὰ σώματα, καὶ ἐκ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν ἀκμῆς εἰς τὴν ἄκραν ὥραν ὑπερανθήσαντα, τήκεσθαι παρ' αὐτῶν καταβασκαινόμενα, καὶ ὅλον ἀθρόως συναναι ρεῖσθαι τὸν ὄγκον, οἷον ῥεύματός τινος ὀλεθρίου ἐκ τῶν φθονερῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἀποῤῥέοντος, καὶ λυμαινομένου καὶ διαφθείροντος. Ἐγὼ δὲ τοῦτον μὲν τὸν λόγον ἀποπέμπομαι, ὡς δημώδη καὶ τῇ γυναικωνίτιδι παρεισαχθέντα ὑπὸ γραϊδίων· ἐκεῖνο δέ φημι, ὅτι οἱ μισόκαλοι δαίμονες, ἐπειδὰν οἰκείας ἑαυτοῖς εὕρωσι προαιρέσεις, παντοίως αὐταῖς πρὸς τὸ ἴδιον ἀποκέχρηνται βούλημα· ὥστε καὶ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς τῶν βασκάνων εἰς ὑπηρεσίαν χρῆσθαι τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος. Εἶτα οὐ φρίσσεις ὑπηρέτην σεαυτὸν ποιῶν δαίμονος ὀλεθρίου, ἀλλ' ὑποδέχῃ κα κὸν, δι' οὗ ἐχθρὸς μὲν γενήσῃ τῶν μηδὲν ἀδικούντων, ἐχθρὸς δὲ Θεοῦ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ ἀφθόνου; Φύγωμεν κακὸν ἀφόρητον. Ὄφεώς ἐστι δίδαγμα, δαιμόνων εὕρημα, ἐχθροῦ ἐπισπορὰ, ἀῤῥαβὼν κο λάσεως, ἐμπόδιον εὐσεβείας, ὁδὸς ἐπὶ γέενναν, στέ ρησις βασιλείας. Δῆλοι δέ πως καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ προσώπῳ τυγχάνουσιν οἱ φθονοῦντες. Ὄμμα τούτοις ξηρὸν καὶ ἀλαμπὲς, παρειὰ κατηφὴς, ὁφρὺς συμπε πτωκυῖα, ἡ ψυχὴ τῷ πάθει συγκεχυμένη, τὸ τῆς ἀληθείας κριτήριον ἐπὶ τῶν πραγμάτων οὐκ ἔχουσα. Οὐ πρᾶξις κατ' ἀρετὴν ἐπαινετὴ παρ' ἐκείνοις, οὐ λόγου δύναμις σεμνότητι κεκοσμημένη καὶ χάρισιν, οὐκ ἄλλο τι τῶν ζηλωτῶν καὶ περιβλέπτων οὐδέν. Ὥσπερ δὲ οἱ γῦπες πρὸς τὰ δυσώδη φέρονται, πολ λοὺς μὲν λειμῶνας, πολλοὺς δὲ ἡδεῖς καὶ εὐώδεις τόπους ὑπεριπτάμενοι· καὶ αἱ μυῖαι τὸ μὲν ὑγιαῖνον παρατρέχουσι, πρὸς δὲ τὸ ἕλκος ἐπείγονται· οὕτως οἱ βάσκανοι τὰς μὲν τοῦ βίου λαμπρότητας καὶ τὰ μεγέθη τῶν κατορθουμένων οὐδὲ προσβλέπουσι, τοῖς δὲ σαθροῖς ἐπιτίθενται· κἄν τι προσπταῖσαι συμβῇ, οἷα πολλὰ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα, τοῦτο δημοσιεύουσι, καὶ ἀπὸ τούτων τοὺς ἄνδρας γνωρίζειν βούλονται· ὥσπερ οἱ πονηροὶ τῶν ζωγράφων ἀπὸ τῆς ἐνδιαστρόφου ῥινὸς, ἢ ἀπό τινος οὐλῆς ἢ κολοβώματος, ἐκ φύσεως ἢ ἐκ πάθους ἐπισυμβάντος, τὰς μορφὰς τῶν γραφομένων ἀποσημαίνοντες. Δεινοὶ δὲ ταῖς εἰς τὸ χεῖρον παρατροπαῖς τὸ ἐπαινετὸν διαπτύσαι, καὶ ἐκ τῆς γείτονος κακίας τὴν ἀρετὴν διαβαλεῖν. Θρασὺν μὲν γὰρ λέγουσι τὸν ἀνδρεῖον, ἀνάλγητον δὲ τὸν σώφρονα· τὸν δίκαιον ἀπηνῆ· κακοῦργον τὸν φρόνιμον. Καὶ τὸν μεγαλοπρεπῆ μὲν ὡς βάναυσον δια βάλλουσι, τὸν ἐλευθέριον δὲ ὡς ἄσωτον· πάλιν τὸν οἰκονομικὸν φειδωλόν. Καὶ ὅλως, πάντα τὰ τῆς ἀρε τῆς εἴδη οὐκ ἀπορεῖ παρ' αὐτοῖς ὀνόματος ἐκ τῆς ἀντικειμένης κακίας μετενεχθέντος.
thought_title: Envy harms the envious, not the envied
orientation: Basil is describing how envy works in the envious person, arguing that it destroys the one who harbors it rather than the one it targets.
pass_a_gloss: That very thing at least one might praise in the evil, that by however much more violently it is stirred, by so much more grievous it is to the one who possesses it. For just as of arrows the ones carried forcefully, whenever they fall upon something strong and resistant, return upon the one who sent them; so also the movements of envy, in no way grieving the one envied, become blows of the envious person himself. For who by grieving ever diminished the good things of his neighbor? Himself indeed he consumed in addition, wasting away with griefs. And already even more destructive than the venomous creatures themselves are those sick with envy thought to be; since those creatures through a wound inject the venom, and little by little with putrefaction consume the bitten part; but the envious, some suppose, cast the harm even through the eyes alone; so that healthy bodies, and from the prime of age blooming into the height of beauty, waste away being envied by them, and the whole bulk is destroyed all at once, as if some destructive stream flows from the envious eyes, and ruins and destroys. But I dismiss this account, as popular and introduced into the women's quarters by old wives; but that I say, that the hateful demons, whenever they find choices suited to themselves, use them in every way for their own purpose; so that they also use the eyes of the envious for the service of their own will. Then do you not shudder, making yourself a servant of a destructive demon, but do you welcome an evil, through which you will become an enemy of those who do no wrong, and an enemy of God the good and ungrudging? Let us flee an evil unbearable. It is the serpent's teaching, a discovery of demons, a sowing of the enemy, a down payment of punishment, a hindrance of piety, a road to Gehenna, a deprivation of the kingdom. And clear somehow even in their very face are those who envy. The eye for these is dry and without light, the cheek downcast, the brow fallen together, the soul confused by the passion, not having the criterion of truth in matters. No deed according to virtue is praiseworthy among them, no power of speech adorned with dignity and graces, nor any other of the things worthy of emulation and admired. But just as vultures are carried toward foul-smelling things, flying over many meadows and many sweet and fragrant places; and flies pass by the healthy part, but hurry toward the wound; so the envious do not even look at the splendors of life and the greatness of achievements, but attack the rotten parts; and if some stumble happens to occur, such as many human things, this they make public, and from these things they want to know the men; just as the wicked among painters, from a crooked nose, or from some scar or mutilation, from nature or from a mishap that occurred, marking out the forms of those being painted. And they are clever at spitting upon the praiseworthy by distortions toward the worse, and at slandering virtue from the neighboring vice. For bold they call the courageous man, and unfeeling the self-controlled; the just man harsh; the prudent man a schemer. And the magnificent man they slander as vulgar, and the generous man as wasteful; again the thrifty man as stingy. And in general, all the forms of virtue do not lack among them a name transferred from the opposite vice.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'envy' for βασκανία; keeps the passion term consistent throughout the homily.
Renders the adjective as a substantive for the envious people, matching the glossary's 'envious person' for βάσκανος.
μισόκαλος means 'hating the good'; 'hateful demons' captures the demons' hostility to what is good while keeping the glossary's 'demons'.
ἄφθονος is the negative of φθόνος; 'ungrudging' preserves the wordplay with envy that 'without envy' would make too explicit.
ἀρραβών is a commercial term for a pledge or first installment; 'down payment' keeps the financial metaphor Basil uses.
ἐπισπορά means something sown on top or in addition; 'a sowing' preserves the agricultural image of the enemy planting envy.

pass_b_english: One thing, at least, someone might even praise in this evil: the more violently it is stirred, the more grievous it becomes to the one who possesses it. For just as arrows shot with force, when they strike something hard and resistant, rebound upon the one who hurled them, so the movements of envy, causing no grief to the person envied, become blows upon the envious person himself. For who, by grieving, ever diminished his neighbor's good things? He only consumed himself, wasting away with sorrow. Indeed, those sick with envy are thought to be more destructive than venomous creatures themselves. For those creatures inject their poison through a wound, and little by little the corruption eats away what has been bitten. But some suppose that the envious inflict harm through their eyes alone, so that vigorous bodies, blooming in the full flower of their youthful prime, waste away under their envious gaze, and their whole bulk is suddenly destroyed, as if a deadly stream flowed from the envious eyes, defiling and destroying. I dismiss that account as a popular tale brought into the women's quarters by old wives. But this I do say: the hateful demons, when they find choices suited to themselves, use those choices in every way for their own purpose, so that they even employ the eyes of envious people in the service of their own will. Do you not shudder, then, at making yourself the servant of a deadly demon? Do you welcome an evil through which you will become an enemy of those who have done no wrong, and an enemy of God, who is good and ungrudging? Let us flee this unbearable evil. It is the serpent's teaching, the demons' invention, the enemy's sowing, a down payment of punishment, a hindrance to piety, a road to Gehenna, a loss of the kingdom. The envious are somehow recognizable even by their very face. Their eye is dry and dim, their cheek downcast, their brow contracted; their soul is thrown into confusion by the passion, and does not hold the standard of truth in judging matters. No action done according to virtue is praiseworthy among them, no power of speech adorned with dignity and grace, nothing else that is admired and esteemed. Just as vultures are drawn to foul smells, flying over many meadows and many pleasant, fragrant places, and flies pass by what is healthy and hurry to a wound, so the envious do not even look at the splendors of life or the greatness of noble achievements, but fasten on what is rotten. And if someone happens to stumble—as often happens in human affairs—they make it public, and from such things they want to identify the man. They are like wicked painters who mark the forms of their subjects by a crooked nose, or by some scar or mutilation, whether from nature or from some accident. They are skilled at twisting things for the worse, at spitting on what is praiseworthy, and at slandering virtue by means of a neighboring vice. For they call the courageous man reckless, and the self-controlled man unfeeling; the just man harsh, the prudent man a schemer. They slander the magnificent man as vulgar, and the generous man as a spendthrift; again, the thrifty man they call miserly. In short, every form of virtue does not lack among them a name borrowed from the opposite vice.
notes: The source contains several line-break hyphenations (φερό μενα, ὑπονε νόηνται, συναναι ρεῖσθαι, κα κὸν, κο λάσεως, στέ ρησις, συμπε πτωκυῖα, πολ λοὺς, δια βάλλουσι, ἀρε τῆς) which have been resolved in the gloss.

problems.quote: the corruption spreads over what has been bitten
problems.source_quote: κατὰ μικρὸν σηπεδόσι τὸ δηχθὲν ἐπινέμεται
problems.why: ἐπινέμεται means 'is consumed/eaten away,' not 'spreads over.' The bitten thing is eaten away, not covered.
problems.fix: little by little the corruption eats away what was bitten
problems.ruling: ἐπινέμεται means 'grazes upon/devours,' not 'spreads over'; subject is corruption eating the bitten thing.

edits.old: little by little the corruption spreads over what has been bitten
edits.new: little by little the corruption eats away what has been bitten

fixed: Corrected 'spreads over' to 'eats away' for ἐπινέμεται, which means 'is consumed/eaten away,' not 'spreads over.'

last_rejected.quote: the more grievous it becomes to the one who possesses it
last_rejected.why: κεκτημένῳ means 'the one possessing it' (the envious person), but context shows envy harms its possessor; however, 'possesses' is awkward—envy possesses the person, not vice versa. The sense is slightly off: it becomes more grievous to the one whom envy holds/who is subject to it.
last_rejected.fix: the more grievous its effect on the one in whom it dwells
last_rejected.ruling: κεκτημένῳ = 'the one possessing it'; envy as a possession harming its possessor is standard Greek idiom. Translation captures the meaning correctly.

last_rejected.quote: blooming in the full flower of their youthful prime
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν ἀκμῆς εἰς τὴν ἄκραν ὥραν ὑπερανθήσαντα
last_rejected.why: ὑπερανθήσαντα means 'having bloomed above/beyond,' not 'in the full flower.' The bodies have bloomed past their prime into extreme beauty; 'youthful prime' misrepresents the peak being surpassed.
last_rejected.fix: having bloomed beyond the prime of life into supreme beauty
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπερανθήσαντα = 'having bloomed beyond'; 'blooming in full flower of youthful prime' is within normal rendering range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: nothing else that is admired and esteemed
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐκ ἄλλο τι τῶν ζηλωτῶν καὶ περιβλέπτων οὐδέν
last_rejected.why: ζηλωτῶν here means 'emulated/zealously admired,' but περιβλέπτων means 'looked-around-at, conspicuous, notable'—things that draw all eyes. 'Esteemed' weakens the visual/conspicuous sense.
last_rejected.fix: nothing else that is zealously emulated and conspicuously admired
last_rejected.ruling: περιβλέπτων ranges from 'conspicuous' to 'esteemed'; 'esteemed' is within normal meaning and not misleading here.

last_rejected.quote: They are like wicked painters who mark the forms of their subjects by a crooked nose
last_rejected.source_quote: ὥσπερ οἱ πονηροὶ τῶν ζωγράφων ἀπὸ τῆς ἐνδιαστρόφου ῥινός... τὰς μορφὰς τῶν γραφομένων ἀποσημαίνοντες
last_rejected.why: ἀποσημαίνοντες means 'indicate, point out, identify,' not 'mark' (as in paint/mark on). The painters identify/recognize forms by a flaw, not mark them with it. 'Mark' is ambiguous—could mean 'stain' or 'identify.'
last_rejected.fix: who identify the forms of their subjects by a crooked nose
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποσημαίνοντες ranges from 'indicate' to 'mark/distinguish'; 'mark' is within normal range and context is clear.

last_rejected.quote: They are skilled at twisting things for the worse, at spitting on what is praiseworthy
last_rejected.source_quote: Δεινοὶ δὲ ταῖς εἰς τὸ χεῖρον παρατροπαῖς τὸ ἐπαινετὸν διαπτύσαι
last_rejected.why: The syntax shows δεινοὶ + dative (ταῖς... παρατροπαῖς) + infinitive: 'skilled at/through distortions toward the worse to spit on what is praiseworthy.' The English splits this but omits that the 'spitting' is accomplished by/through the distortions; 'at twisting... at spitting' makes them separate skills rather than one.
last_rejected.fix: They are skilled, through distortions toward the worse, at spitting on what is praiseworthy
last_rejected.ruling: δεινοὶ + dative + infinitive rendered as two coordinated skills is a stylistic choice; core meaning of both skills is preserved.
